content.text: Book reference: Chapter 12, pages 389–445. Guided Exercises: Validating Network Configuration, Configuring Networking from the Command Line, Editing Network Configuration Files, Configuring Host Names and Name Resolution. Lab: Managing Networking.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This whole chapter
Setting a static IP with nmcli, setting the hostname, and configuring name resolution are core, hands-on RHCSA tasks — arguably as central to the exam as user management and permissions.
Layer
Job
Examples
Application
How programs talk to each other
SSH, HTTPS, NFS/CIFS, SMTP
Transport
TCP (reliable, connection-oriented) or UDP (connectionless) — combined with an IP address, a port forms a socket
Port list in /etc/services
Internet
Moves data from source host to destination host; routers connect networks
IPv4, IPv6
Link
Physical/local-segment delivery; each device has a hardware MAC address
Ethernet (802.3), WLAN (802.11)
Interface naming — why eth0 went away

Older RHEL used eth0, eth1... based purely on detection order — but detection order isn't guaranteed to stay consistent across reboots or hardware changes, so names could shift unpredictably. RHEL 7+ names interfaces from firmware/PCI-topology information instead, so a given physical port keeps the same name permanently:
Prefix/pattern
Meaning
en / wl / ww
Ethernet / WLAN / WWAN (mobile broadband)
eno1
On-board Ethernet device, firmware index 1
ens3
Ethernet card in PCI hotplug slot 3
enp0s1
Ethernet, PCI bus 0, slot 1
enp0s1f0 / enp0s1f1
Function 0 / function 1 of a multi-port card at that same bus/slot
NOTE —
The trade-off of persistent naming: you can no longer assume a single-NIC machine will be called eth0 (or even ens3) — check with ip link show rather than guessing from convention.

A 32-bit address, written as four dot-separated octets (0–255 each), splits into a network part and a host part. The prefix (netmask) says how many leading bits belong to the network. All hosts sharing a network part can reach each other directly, with no router needed; every host part must be unique within that network.
Address
Prefix
Network address
Broadcast address
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Be fluent converting prefix ↔ netmask ↔ network/broadcast address without a calculator

The network address is the host part all-zeros; the broadcast address is the host part all-ones. This exact calculation is a standard exam sub-task inside larger networking questions — practice it on odd prefixes like /19 and /27, not just the easy /24 and /8.
127.0.0.1 (and the whole 127.0.0.0/8 network) always refers back to the local system itself — "localhost" — regardless of any real network interface.
IPv4 routing

Every host keeps a routing table: destination network, which local interface to send through, and (if needed) an intermediate router's address. The most specific matching entry wins — if two routes both match a destination, the one with the longer/more specific prefix is used. Anything matching nothing more specific falls to the default route, 0.0.0.0/0, which points at a router reachable via one of the host's own more-specific routes.
ip route
# default via 192.168.5.254 dev enp3s0 proto static metric 1024
# 192.168.5.0/24 dev enp3s0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.5.10

A router does the same lookup as any host, but instead of discarding traffic not addressed to it, forwards that traffic onward per its own table — this forward-and-repeat process is exactly how a packet crosses multiple networks to reach a distant destination.
128 bits, written as eight colon-separated groups of four hex digits. RHEL runs dual-stack by default — IPv4 and IPv6 active side by side on the same interface.
Shortening rule
Example
Leading zeros in a group may be dropped
One run of consecutive all-zero groups may collapse to :: (once per address, maximum)
⚠ WARNING — A port after an IPv6 address needs brackets
[2001:db8:0:10::1]:80 — without the brackets, the port number looks like it's part of the address itself and parses incorrectly.
Address / network
IPv4 equivalent
Meaning
localhost
The unspecified address — e.g. a service listening on every configured address
The default route

Unlike IPv4, IPv6 uses a standard /64 subnet size almost everywhere — half the address is network prefix, half is interface ID, leaving effectively unlimited hosts per subnet. A provider typically allocates a shorter prefix (e.g. /48) to an organization, leaving room to carve out many /64 subnets from it.
Command
Shows
ip link show
Every interface, its state (UP/DOWN), and MAC address
ip addr show [dev]
IPv4/IPv6 addresses and prefixes on one or all interfaces
ip -s link show dev
RX/TX packet, error, and drop counters — a first stop for suspected network issues
ping -c3 host
Basic reachability (IPv4); ping6 for IPv6 — always use -c to cap the count, or it runs until Ctrl+C
ip route / ip -6 route
The IPv4 / IPv6 routing table
tracepath host
Traces the hop-by-hop path to a destination — identifies which router along the way is the problem
NOTE — Pinging a link-local address needs a zone identifier
ping6 ff02::1%ens3 — link-local addresses aren't globally unique, so you must tell ping6 which interface to send out of (after the %). Omitting it produces "connect: Invalid argument".
NetworkManager is the daemon that owns network configuration; nmcli is the command-line tool that talks to it. Two concepts to keep straight:
Term
Meaning
Device
A physical or virtual network interface (e.g. ens3)
Connection

A named bundle of settings that CAN be applied to a device — only one connection is active per device at a time, but several can exist for the same device (e.g. "work-wifi" vs. "home-wifi" for the same wireless card)
Configuration is saved under /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-<name>, named after the connection, not the device.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — The core nmcli command set — memorize this table
Every row here is a standalone exam-relevant task.
Task
Command
Show all devices and their state
nmcli dev status
List all connections
nmcli con show
List only active connections
nmcli con show --active
Show every setting for one connection
nmcli con show NAME
Create a DHCP connection
nmcli con add con-name NAME type ethernet ifname DEV
Create a static IPv4 connection
nmcli con add con-name NAME type ethernet ifname DEV ip4 IP/PREFIX gw4 GATEWAY
Modify a setting on an EXISTING connection
nmcli con mod NAME ipv4.addresses "IP/PREFIX GATEWAY"
Add one value without replacing the list
nmcli con mod NAME +ipv4.dns IP
Activate a connection
nmcli con up NAME
Deactivate AND disconnect a device (the correct way to bring an interface down)
nmcli dev dis DEV
Reload config files after manual edits
nmcli con reload
Delete a connection (and its ifcfg file)
nmcli con del NAME
⚠ WARNING — nmcli con down vs. nmcli dev disconnect — a genuine gotcha

Most wired connections have autoconnect enabled by default. nmcli con down NAME brings the connection down, but since the device is still present and available, NetworkManager immediately reactivates it (or another matching connection) right back up. nmcli dev disconnect DEV is the command that actually keeps an interface down, because it disconnects the device itself, not just one connection bound to it.
⚠ WARNING — Switching from DHCP to static requires changing the method, not just adding an address

Setting ipv4.addresses on a connection that's still ipv4.method auto doesn't fully switch it to static — the connection may hang, fail to activate cleanly, or end up with BOTH a DHCP-assigned address and your static one. Always set ipv4.method manual (or ipv6.method manual) explicitly when moving off DHCP.

nmcli con show NAME output distinguishes two kinds of settings by case: lowercase fields (like ipv4.addresses) are static properties you set and that persist in the ifcfg file; ALL-CAPS fields are live, temporary values (e.g. from DHCP) that aren't stored anywhere permanent.

Who can change network settings: root always can. A regular user logged in AT the physical console (not over SSH) can also make many changes — the reasoning is that physical presence at a laptop/workstation implies a legitimate need to switch wifi networks on the fly; SSH-connected regular users cannot, without becoming root. nmcli gen permissions shows exactly what your current session is allowed to do.
Command
Effect
hostname
Shows (or, given an argument, TEMPORARILY changes) the current hostname — doesn't survive reboot
hostnamectl set-hostname NAME
Sets the PERSISTENT static hostname, stored in /etc/hostname
hostnamectl status
Full detail: static hostname, OS, kernel, virtualization, machine/boot IDs
⚠ WARNING — hostname alone doesn't persist — a real, testable distinction

sudo hostname newname changes the running system's hostname immediately, but /etc/hostname is untouched — reboot and the old name comes right back. Only hostnamectl set-hostname updates /etc/hostname for a change that survives a reboot.
Name resolution order
The stub resolver checks /etc/hosts FIRST (order controlled by /etc/nsswitch.conf), then falls back to DNS servers listed in /etc/resolv.conf if no match is found there.
# /etc/hosts:
127.0.0.1 localhost
172.25.250.10 servera.lab.example.com servera
# /etc/resolv.conf (normally generated by NetworkManager — don't hand-edit if using DHCP/nmcli):
search example.com
nameserver 172.25.254.254
Command
Effect
getent hosts NAME
Tests resolution specifically via /etc/hosts
host NAME
Tests resolution via DNS directly, forward or reverse
nmcli con mod NAME ipv4.dns IP
Set the DNS server(s) for a connection (replaces the list — use +ipv4.dns to add one instead)
nmcli con mod NAME ipv4.ignore-auto-dns yes
Stop DHCP from overwriting your manually-set DNS servers in /etc/resolv.conf
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — A DNS change needs a con down/up (or reload) to actually take effect

Editing DNS settings with nmcli con mod alone updates the ifcfg file, but the running connection doesn't pick it up until you reactivate it — nmcli con down NAME; nmcli con up NAME (or nmcli con reload for file-based edits).

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: 1. ssh student@servera; ip addr show — identify the interface name, current IP, and prefix.
2. sudo nmcli con show — note the connection NAME (often not identical to the device name).
3. sudo nmcli con mod <NAME> ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses "172.25.250.10/24" ipv4.gateway 172.25.250.254 — then nmcli con down <NAME>; nmcli con up <NAME> to apply it.
4. ip addr show to confirm the static address took effect; ping -c3 workstation to confirm connectivity survived the change.
5. hostnamectl status — confirm the static hostname matches servera.lab.example.com from Part 0's setup.
6. getent hosts bastion and host bastion.lab.example.com — compare /etc/hosts-based vs DNS-style resolution on your lab (which has no real DNS server, so only the /etc/hosts lookup will succeed).
1. Q1 — Calculate the network address and broadcast address for 10.20.30.40/22.
2. Q2 — You run nmcli con down office-wifi to take a laptop's wifi offline, but it reconnects within a second. What's actually happening, and what command achieves what you intended?
3. Q3 — You set ipv4.addresses on a connection to a static IP but leave ipv4.method as auto. What goes wrong, and what's the fix?
NOTE — Answers

Q1 — /22 = 255.255.252.0. 30 in binary is 00011110; the /22 boundary falls within the third octet, masking to 00011100 = 28. Network address: 10.20.28.0. Broadcast address (host part all-ones): 10.20.31.255.

Q2 — Autoconnect is enabled on that connection, so as soon as NetworkManager sees the device is still present and available, it reactivates the connection right back up. nmcli dev disconnect <device-name> disconnects the DEVICE itself, which actually stays down.

Q3 — The connection may fail to activate cleanly, hang, or end up with both a DHCP address and the static one simultaneously, since it's still trying to also negotiate DHCP. Fix: explicitly set ipv4.method manual alongside the static address.

The TCP/IP model (application/transport/internet/link) describes how data moves between hosts; modern RHEL interface names (en/wl/ww + firmware/PCI info) are persistent, unlike the old eth0-style detection-order names.
An IPv4 address + prefix determines its network and broadcast address; the most specific matching route wins, with 0.0.0.0/0 as the catch-all default.
IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, mostly /64 subnets, and RHEL runs IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack by default.

nmcli manages devices (physical/virtual interfaces) and connections (named setting bundles) — con mod for static settings, dev disconnect (not con down) to actually keep an interface offline, and ipv4.method manual whenever moving off DHCP.
hostnamectl set-hostname persists to /etc/hostname; plain hostname does not. /etc/hosts is checked before /etc/resolv.conf's DNS servers for name resolution.
